docs.title: Slick Seeker
docs.text: Type-safe, high-performance cursor-based pagination for Slick 3.5+.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Keyset Pagination - O(1) performance regardless of page depth
  • Bidirectional - Navigate forward and backward through result sets
  • Type-Safe - Compile-time verification of cursor/column matching
  • Count-Free Pagination - Skip COUNT(*) queries with pageWithoutCount
  • PostgreSQL Tuple Optimization - Compile-time safe tuple comparisons for PostgreSQL
  • Profile Agnostic - Works with any Slick JDBC profile (PostgreSQL, MySQL, H2, SQLite, Oracle, etc.)
  • Flexible Ordering - Support for nulls first/last, custom enum orders
  • Modular - Core + optional Play JSON integration
  • Composable - Chain decorators for Base64, compression, encryption

docs.title: Why Cursor-Based Pagination?
docs.text:
Traditional offset-based pagination (OFFSET + LIMIT) has serious performance issues:

-- Page 1000: Database must scan and skip 19,900 rows!
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY name LIMIT 100 OFFSET 19900;

Problems:

  • Slow for deep pages (O(n) where n = offset)
  • Unstable with concurrent writes (items shift between pages)
  • Memory intensive for large offsets

Cursor-based pagination (keyset pagination) solves this:

-- Any page: Fast index-based lookup!
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE name > 'last_name' OR (name = 'last_name' AND id > last_id)
ORDER BY name, id 
LIMIT 100;

Benefits:

  • Constant O(1) performance for any page
  • Stable with concurrent writes
  • Efficient index usage

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your build.sbt:

libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "io.github.devnico" %% "slick-seeker" % "0.7.2",
  "io.github.devnico" %% "slick-seeker-play-json" % "0.7.2"  // Optional, but you need some kind of cursor encoder
)

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
// Step 1: Create a custom profile
import slick.jdbc.PostgresProfile
import io.github.devnico.slickseeker.SlickSeekerSupport
import io.github.devnico.slickseeker.playjson.PlayJsonSeekerSupport

trait MyPostgresProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits
  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

object MyPostgresProfile extends MyPostgresProfile

// Step 2: Import your profile API
import MyPostgresProfile.api._

// Step 3: Define your table
case class User(id: Int, name: String, email: String)

class Users(tag: Tag) extends Table[User](tag, "users") {
  def id = column[Int]("id", O.PrimaryKey, O.AutoInc)
  def name = column[String]("name")
  def email = column[String]("email")
  def * = (id, name, email).mapTo[User]
}

val users = TableQuery[Users]

// Create a seeker
val seeker = users.toSeeker
  .seek(_.name.asc)      // Primary sort
  .seek(_.id.asc)        // Tiebreaker

// Paginate (with total count)
val page1 = db.run(seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = None))
// PaginatedResult(total=100, items=[...], nextCursor=Some("..."), prevCursor=None)

// Paginate (without total count — skips the COUNT(*) query)
val fast1 = db.run(seeker.pageWithoutCount(limit = 20, cursor = None))
// PaginatedResultWithoutCount(items=[...], nextCursor=Some("..."), prevCursor=None)

val page2 = db.run(seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = page1.nextCursor))
// Continue pagination...

docs.title: Cursor-Based Pagination
docs.text: Slick Seeker implements keyset pagination, which uses the values from the last row as a cursor to find the next page.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Instead of using OFFSET:

-- Slow for deep pages
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY name LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000;

We use the last row's values:

-- Fast for any page
SELECT * FROM users 
WHERE name > 'last_name' OR (name = 'last_name' AND id > last_id)
ORDER BY name, id 
LIMIT 20;

docs.title: seek()
docs.text:
Use seek() for direct column references.

// Direct columns - automatic extraction
val seeker = users.toSeeker
  .seek(_.name.asc)
  .seek(_.id.asc)

Works with:

  • Table columns: _.name, _.email
  • Tuple fields: _._1, _._2
  • Nested tuples: _._1._2
  • Any computed column: _.name.toLowerCase

The SQL looks like:

SELECT t.*, t.name, t.id  -- Cursor columns added automatically
FROM users t
WHERE t.name > ? OR (t.name = ? AND t.id > ?)
ORDER BY t.name ASC, t.id ASC
LIMIT 20

docs.title: Cursor Values as Parameters
docs.text:
Cursor values are bound as parameters of the column's type, so they compare exactly like the column's own values (a REAL column's 0.1f equals its cursor value, which the literal 0.1 would not). Cursor value codecs should therefore decode the column's type; values of another type are written as literals, as in earlier versions. Floating-point seek columns stay fragile where the driver sends parameters as text (MySQL's and MariaDB's drivers by default, see below and Supported Databases); prefer DECIMAL columns where you can.

  • On SQL Server, a cursor value only compares like its column sorts if it has the column's type, and the driver binds strings as nvarchar and timestamps as datetime2. Seekers therefore cast cursor values of string columns to VARCHAR(MAX) or NVARCHAR(MAX) and of DATETIME / SMALLDATETIME columns to their type, after the column's declared type: its O.SqlType, else the type Slick's DDL gives it (VARCHAR for strings, DATETIME2(6) for timestamps). Declare O.SqlType on seek columns whose database type differs, e.g. column[String]("name", O.SqlType("NVARCHAR(100)")) or column[LocalDateTime]("at", O.SqlType("DATETIME")). An expression gets the declared type of its columns of the same type (_.name.toLowerCase: name's). Values of an expression over columns of different declared types, or of a column of a query the seeker can't follow to its table, are not cast: they compare as the driver binds them (nvarchar, datetime2). Override seekerCursorValueCast in your profile to change the casts.

  • On SQL Server, cursor columns are selected as expressions, and so are columns the items select more than once (pageAs(t => (t.id, t.id))): SQL Server resolves order by "id" against the selected columns and fails with "Ambiguous column name" if one is selected twice.

  • On MySQL and MariaDB, the drivers send Float parameters as text by default, and 0.1 as a DOUBLE never equals a single-precision FLOAT column's 0.1f; they also send FLOAT values as text with 6 significant digits. Seekers therefore cast cursor values of FLOAT columns (declared with O.SqlType("FLOAT"), or FLOAT(p) up to p = 24) to FLOAT and select the column as DOUBLE for the cursor, which needs MySQL 8.0.17+ or MariaDB 10.4.5+. Slick's DDL declares Float as REAL, which is DOUBLE there: not cast (see the MariaDB limitation in Supported Databases). On MySQL, seekerCursorValueCast types are written as CAST(? AS type), so they must be types MySQL's CAST takes.

  • On PostgreSQL, string-backed cursor values (String and types mapped to String) are bound untyped, as literals would be, so they compare with native enums, uuid and other columns mapped to String. Override seekerUntypedStringParams in your profile to change it.

  • With parameters, every page of a seeker has the same SQL, so the database may reuse a generic plan (PostgreSQL does after five executions of a server-side prepared statement). Check the plans of hot page queries; plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan restores planning per cursor value.
  • The settings (seekerRowComparisons, seekerUntypedStringParams, seekerCursorValueCast, seekerDefaultNulls) are read from the profile a page runs with: the implicit profile of page / pageWithoutCount, or the profile of a CompiledSeekPage.

docs.title: Row Value Comparisons
docs.text:
On PostgreSQL and H2, when all seek columns are non-nullable and sort in the same direction, the seeker compares them as one row value:

WHERE (t.name, t.id) > (?, ?)   -- instead of t.name > ? OR (t.name = ? AND t.id > ?)
ORDER BY t.name ASC, t.id ASC

The results are the same, and the database can scan a composite index on (name, id) from the cursor on. Seekers with Option columns, mixed directions or custom ColumnSeekFilters chain their conditions instead. To turn row value comparisons off (or on for another database), override them in your profile:

trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile with SlickSeekerSupport {
  override def seekerRowComparisons: Boolean = false
  // …
}

Check the plans before turning them on elsewhere: MySQL and MariaDB support row values but don't use an index range for them the way they do for the chained conditions, so keep them off there.

docs.title: Null Handling
docs.text:
Slick Seeker supports explicit null ordering:

.seek(_.lastName.nullsLast.asc)   // Nulls last
.seek(_.lastName.nullsFirst.asc)  // Nulls first

// Without a nulls clause: where the database puts nulls by default
.seek(_.lastName.asc)

Without a nulls clause, an Option column's nulls go where the database puts them by default, and the seeker writes that ordering out explicitly so its cursor conditions match it:

Database .asc .desc PostgreSQL, Oracle, DB2, Derby (and unknown databases) nulls last nulls first H2, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server nulls first nulls last HSQLDB nulls first nulls first

Custom ColumnSeekFilters on Option columns and expressions get this ordering too, so they always see an explicit NullsFirst / NullsLast there; on non-null columns they keep NullsDefault, also on backward pages.

This keeps the order (and the indexes serving it) the database uses anyway. If your database or its configuration sorts nulls differently, override seekerDefaultNulls in your profile: e.g. H2 with DEFAULT_NULL_ORDERING, or PostgreSQL-compatible databases with other defaults that use PostgresProfile (CockroachDB sorts nulls first ascending, like H2). A wrong placement still pages every row exactly once (with custom filters, if they follow the nulls ordering they get), but puts null rows elsewhere than the database would and can't use an index for the order:

trait MyProfile extends H2Profile with SlickSeekerSupport {
  // H2 with DEFAULT_NULL_ORDERING=HIGH
  override def seekerDefaultNulls(direction: slick.ast.Ordering.Direction): slick.ast.Ordering.NullOrdering =
    if (direction == slick.ast.Ordering.Asc) slick.ast.Ordering.NullsLast else slick.ast.Ordering.NullsFirst
  // …
}

For CockroachDB (which uses PostgresProfile), the reverse:

trait MyCockroachProfile extends PostgresProfile with SlickSeekerSupport {
  override def seekerDefaultNulls(direction: slick.ast.Ordering.Direction): slick.ast.Ordering.NullOrdering =
    if (direction == slick.ast.Ordering.Asc) slick.ast.Ordering.NullsFirst else slick.ast.Ordering.NullsLast
  // …
}

seekDirection keeps explicit null orderings when a column already sorts in that direction and mirrors them when it reverses it (.desc.nullsFirst becomes .asc.nullsLast). Columns without one keep the database's default for the new direction, as if they had been declared with it:

// Same as .seek(_.lastName.desc): nulls where the database puts them for DESC
.seek(_.lastName)
.seekDirection(SortDirection.Desc)

docs.title: Complex Null Handling
docs.text:
case class Person(
  id: Int,
  firstName: String,
  middleName: Option[String],
  lastName: Option[String]
)

// Sort: lastName (nulls last), middleName (nulls first), firstName, id
val seeker = persons.toSeeker
  .seek(_.lastName.nullsLast.asc)
  .seek(_.middleName.nullsFirst.asc)
  .seek(_.firstName.asc)
  .seek(_.id.asc)

docs.title: Custom Sort Orders (Enums/ADTs)
docs.text:
For enums or sealed traits, define a custom sort order:

Scala 3Scala 2 
enum Status {
  case Pending, Active, Completed, Archived
}

// Define the order
given SeekOrder[Status] = SeekOrder(IndexedSeq(
  Status.Pending,
  Status.Active,
  Status.Completed,
  Status.Archived
))

// Use it
val seeker = tasks.toSeeker
  .seek(_.status.asc)  // Uses custom order
  .seek(_.id.asc)

sealed trait Status
object Status {
  case object Pending extends Status
  case object Active extends Status
  case object Completed extends Status
  case object Archived extends Status
}

// Define the order
implicit val statusOrder: SeekOrder[Status] = SeekOrder(IndexedSeq(
  Status.Pending,
  Status.Active,
  Status.Completed,
  Status.Archived
))

// Use it
val seeker = tasks.toSeeker
  .seek(_.status.asc)  // Uses custom order
  .seek(_.id.asc)

This converts enum values to integers in SQL:

ORDER BY 
  CASE 
    WHEN status = 'Pending' THEN 0
    WHEN status = 'Active' THEN 1
    WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 2
    WHEN status = 'Archived' THEN 3
  END ASC

docs.title: Supported Databases
docs.text:
CI tests against these databases: many seeker configurations paged forward and backward, ad-hoc and compiled, must return each row exactly once in the database's own order.

Database Tested with Profile Notes PostgreSQL 16 PostgresProfile Row value comparisons; untyped string parameters (enums, uuid) H2 2.4 H2Profile Row value comparisons HSQLDB 2.7 HsqldbProfile SQLite 3.53 SQLiteProfile Derby 10.17 DerbyProfile MySQL 8.4 (Connector/J 9) MySQLProfile FLOAT casts (8.0.17+) MariaDB 11.4 (MariaDB Connector/J 3.5) MySQLProfile FLOAT casts (10.4.5+); see REAL columns below SQL Server 2022 (mssql-jdbc 13) SQLServerProfile Declare O.SqlType where it differs from Slick's (casts) Oracle 23 (Free) OracleProfile CockroachDB 25.4 PostgresProfile Needs the nulls override

sbt test covers H2, HSQLDB and SQLite; the others run in containers (Docker) when selected, e.g. one at a time: SEEKER_DATABASES=sqlserver sbt "core/testOnly io.github.devnico.slickseeker.databases.*" (ids: derby, postgresql, mysql, mariadb, sqlserver, oracle, cockroachdb, or all).

Known limitations:

  • MariaDB, Float in REAL / DOUBLE columns (Slick's default DDL for Float): MariaDB Connector/J's batch inserts store 0.1f as 0.10000000149…, its single inserts and text parameters as 0.1, so the same column can hold both and the Float cursor value can't tell which one its row has: pages repeat. No cast fixes both. Declare such columns FLOAT (O.SqlType("FLOAT"), cast) or DECIMAL, map them to Double, or connect with useServerPrepStmts=true (binary parameters, as batches send them). MySQL's Connector/J sends them as text everywhere, so they page correctly there.
  • SQL Server, sendStringParametersAsUnicode=false: varchar and datetime columns still page correctly, but nvarchar values outside the database's code page are lost before any cast: keep the default (true). The same goes for a varchar column whose collation has another code page than the database default. datetimeParameterType=datetime loses datetime2 precision the same way.
  • SQL Server, text / ntext columns can't be sorted, so they can't be seek columns.
  • MySQL / MariaDB, arithmetic over FLOAT columns (e.g. t.f + 0.1f as a seek column): MySQL computes it as DOUBLE, which a Float cursor value can't match exactly, so pages repeat. Seek on the FLOAT column itself, or map the expression to Double (t.f.asColumnOf[Double] + 0.1).
  • SQL Server, the same whole row selected twice (pageAs(t => (t, t))) still fails with Ambiguous column name. Repeated single columns ((t.id, t.id), (t, t.id)) work.
  • MySQL / MariaDB, row value comparisons are off: they don't use an index range for them (see Row Value Comparisons).

docs.title: Pagination Without Count
docs.text:
By default, page() runs a COUNT(*) query to include the total number of matching rows. Use pageWithoutCount() to skip it:

// With count (runs COUNT(*) + data query)
val result: PaginatedResult[User] =
  db.run(seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = None))

// Without count (runs data query only — faster)
val result: PaginatedResultWithoutCount[User] =
  db.run(seeker.pageWithoutCount(limit = 20, cursor = None))

Both methods produce interoperable cursors. You can convert between result types:

val withoutCount: PaginatedResultWithoutCount[User] = result.withoutCount
val withCount: PaginatedResult[User] = withoutCountResult.withCount(total)

docs.title: Compiled Pages
docs.text:
Slick compiles every query to SQL before running it, which can cost more CPU than the database spends on it, especially for joined queries. A seeker builds a new query for every page, so Slick compiles each page again and its pages cannot be precompiled with Compiled. CompiledSeekPage binds the application parameters, cursor values and limit as parameters of queries compiled once instead:

// Created once (e.g. a val), reused for every request
val byMinAge = CompiledSeekPage[Int]((minAge: ConstColumn[Int]) =>
  persons.filter(_.age >= minAge).toSeeker
    .seek(_.lastName.desc.nullsLast)
    .seek(_.id.asc)
)(p => p.id)

byMinAge.pageWithoutCount(params = 30, limit = 20, cursor = None)   // or .page(…) with a total count
  • The application parameters (AU, here Int) are passed per call; build receives them as Reps. The query may only depend on these parameters: everything else (constants, table and schema names, Scala-side branches) is compiled in. Optional filters need either one CompiledSeekPage per combination or SQL-side handling (p.isEmpty || …).
  • Each form of the page query is compiled once: the first page and, for forward and backward pages, one per combination of None values in nullable cursor columns (maxForms = 1 + 2 × 2^nullable columns, or 1 where cursor pages run as ad-hoc pages).
  • Items and cursors are the same as those of pageWithoutCountAs / pageAs for every cursor the seeker produced, including row value comparisons. A cursor that can't be decoded at all fails like it does for the ad-hoc seeker; one whose values don't decode or don't fit the cursor columns gives the first page (the ad-hoc seeker then pages without a cursor filter, or with one on the leading columns if there are fewer values than columns).
  • Cursor pages bind cursor values as parameters. Where they can't, they run as ad-hoc pages (same items and cursors, compiled per page): for custom SeekerSortKeys without typedType or ColumnSeekFilters without applyParam, and for cursor values a codec decoded as another type than the column's.
  • Generic plans: see Cursor Values as Parameters.
  • The seeker needs at least one seek column.
  • SlickPgTupleSeeker (deprecated) is not supported; toSeeker seekers use row value comparisons where they qualify (see Row Value Comparisons).

docs.title: Bidirectional Pagination
docs.text:
Slick Seeker supports both forward and backward navigation with both page() and pageWithoutCount():

// Forward
val page2 = seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = page1.nextCursor)

// Backward
val backToPage1 = seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = page2.prevCursor)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Cursors encode direction:

  • Forward: > prefix
  • Backward: < prefix

For backward pagination:

  1. Sort order is reversed
  2. Results are retrieved
  3. Results are reversed back to original order

This ensures consistent ordering regardless of direction.

docs.title: Cursor Environment
docs.text:
The cursor environment controls how cursors are encoded. Define it inside your profile:

import io.github.devnico.slickseeker.playjson.PlayJsonSeekerSupport

trait MyPostgresProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {
  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits
  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

Components:

  • Codec: Serializes values (e.g., JSON)
  • Decorator: Transforms final string (e.g., Base64)

docs.title: Decorators
docs.text:
Decorators transform cursor strings. Chain them for multiple transformations:

trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits {
    // Override with custom decorator
    override implicit val cursorEnvironment: CursorEnvironment[JsValue] = 
      CursorEnvironment(jsonCursorCodec, IdentityDecorator())
  }

  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

docs.title: Custom Decorator
docs.text:
class HexDecorator(inner: CursorDecorator = IdentityDecorator()) 
  extends CursorDecorator {

  override def encode(value: String): String = {
    val innerEncoded = inner.encode(value)
    innerEncoded.getBytes.map("%02x".format(_)).mkString
  }

  override def decode(cursor: String): Either[Throwable, String] = {
    Try {
      val bytes = cursor.grouped(2).map(Integer.parseInt(_, 16).toByte).toArray
      new String(bytes)
    }.toEither.flatMap(inner.decode)
  }
}

// Use it
trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits {
    override implicit val cursorEnvironment: CursorEnvironment[JsValue] =
      CursorEnvironment(jsonCursorCodec, Base64Decorator(HexDecorator()))
  }

  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

Decorators are useful for:

  • Base64 - URL-safe encoding
  • Compression - Reduce cursor size
  • Encryption - Hide cursor content
  • Signing - Prevent tampering

docs.title: 1. Always Include a Unique Column
docs.text:
// BAD: Non-unique sort can miss/duplicate items
.seek(_.status)

// GOOD: Include unique tiebreaker
.seek(_.status)
.seek(_.id)

docs.title: 2. Create Composite Indexes
docs.text:
-- Match your seek columns
CREATE INDEX idx_users_name_id ON users(name, id);
CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_status_priority_id ON tasks(status, priority, id);

docs.title: 3. Limit Sort Columns
docs.text: Each sort column adds to the WHERE clause complexity. Use 2-4 columns typically.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: Real-world examples and patterns.

docs.title: REST API Endpoint
docs.text:
import io.github.devnico.slickseeker._
import play.api.mvc._
import play.api.libs.json._

// Import your profile API
import MyPostgresProfile.api._

class UserController @Inject()(
  cc: ControllerComponents,
  db: Database
)(implicit ec: ExecutionContext) extends AbstractController(cc) {

  implicit val userFormat: Format[User] = Json.format[User]

  def list(
    cursor: Option[String],
    limit: Option[Int],
    sort: Option[String]
  ): Action[AnyContent] = Action.async {
    val seeker = sort match {
      case Some("name") => users.toSeeker.seek(_.name.asc).seek(_.id.asc)
      case Some("email") => users.toSeeker.seek(_.email.asc).seek(_.id.asc)
      case _ => users.toSeeker.seek(_.id.asc)
    }

    // Use pageWithoutCount to skip the COUNT(*) query for better performance
    db.run(seeker.pageWithoutCount(limit.getOrElse(20), cursor, maxLimit = 100))
      .map(result => Ok(Json.toJson(result)))

    // Or use page to include the total count
    db.run(seeker.page(limit.getOrElse(20), cursor, maxLimit = 100))
      .map(result => Ok(Json.toJson(result)))
  }
}

docs.title: Filtering with Pagination
docs.text:
def searchUsers(
  nameFilter: Option[String],
  activeOnly: Boolean,
  cursor: Option[String],
  limit: Int
): Future[PaginatedResultWithoutCount[User]] = {

  val baseQuery = users
    .filterOpt(nameFilter)(_.name like _)
    .filterIf(activeOnly)(_.active === true)

  val seeker = baseQuery.toSeeker
    .seek(_.name.asc)
    .seek(_.id.asc)

  // Use pageWithoutCount for filtered queries where the total is less useful
  db.run(seeker.pageWithoutCount(limit, cursor))
}

docs.title: Joined Tables
docs.text:
case class Order(id: Int, userId: Int, total: Double, createdAt: Timestamp)
case class User(id: Int, name: String, email: String)
case class OrderWithUser(order: Order, userName: String)

val ordersWithUsers = orders
  .join(users).on(_.userId === _.id)
  .map { case (o, u) => (o, u.name) }

val seeker = ordersWithUsers.toSeeker
  .seek(t => t._1.createdAt.desc)  // Order by order date
  .seek(t => t._1.id.asc)          // Tiebreaker
  .map { case (order, userName) => 
    OrderWithUser(order, userName)
  }

docs.title: Paging a Selection
docs.text:
Joins needed only for sorting or searching don't have to be selected. pageAs / pageWithoutCountAs page a selection of the element while filtering, sorting and the cursor still use the whole element, e.g. to page ids and load the rows of a page separately. Cursors are the same as those of page / pageWithoutCount.

val seeker = ordersWithUsers.toSeeker
  .seek(t => t._2.asc)      // sort by user name (joined)
  .seek(t => t._1.id.asc)   // tiebreaker

// Selects only the order ids; sorting and cursors still use the joined user name
val idPage: DBIO[PaginatedResultWithoutCount[Int]] =
  seeker.pageWithoutCountAs(limit = 20, cursor = None)(t => t._1.id)

docs.title: Aggregated Results
docs.text:
case class UserStats(userId: Int, orderCount: Int, totalSpent: Double)

val userStats = orders
  .groupBy(_.userId)
  .map { case (userId, orders) =>
    (userId, orders.length, orders.map(_.total).sum)
  }

val seeker = userStats.toSeeker
  .seek(_._3.desc)  // Sort by total spent
  .seek(_._1.asc)   // Tiebreaker: user ID

docs.title: Multi-Level Priority
docs.text:
Scala 3Scala 2 
enum Priority {
  case Critical, High, Normal, Low
}

enum Status {
  case Open, InProgress, Completed
}

given SeekOrder[Priority] = SeekOrder(IndexedSeq(
  Priority.Critical, Priority.High, Priority.Normal, Priority.Low
))

given SeekOrder[Status] = SeekOrder(IndexedSeq(
  Status.Open, Status.InProgress, Status.Completed
))

case class Task(
  id: Int,
  title: String,
  priority: Priority,
  status: Status,
  dueDate: Option[Timestamp]
)

val seeker = tasks.toSeeker
  .seek(_.priority.asc)           // Critical first
  .seek(_.status.asc)             // Open first
  .seek(_.dueDate.nullsLast.asc)  // Due date (overdue first)
  .seek(_.id.asc)                 // Tiebreaker

sealed trait Priority
object Priority {
  case object Critical extends Priority
  case object High extends Priority
  case object Normal extends Priority
  case object Low extends Priority
}

sealed trait Status
object Status {
  case object Open extends Status
  case object InProgress extends Status
  case object Completed extends Status
}

implicit val priorityOrder: SeekOrder[Priority] = SeekOrder(IndexedSeq(
  Priority.Critical, Priority.High, Priority.Normal, Priority.Low
))

implicit val statusOrder: SeekOrder[Status] = SeekOrder(IndexedSeq(
  Status.Open, Status.InProgress, Status.Completed
))

case class Task(
  id: Int,
  title: String,
  priority: Priority,
  status: Status,
  dueDate: Option[Timestamp]
)

val seeker = tasks.toSeeker
  .seek(_.priority.asc)           // Critical first
  .seek(_.status.asc)             // Open first
  .seek(_.dueDate.nullsLast.asc)  // Due date (overdue first)
  .seek(_.id.asc)                 // Tiebreaker

docs.text:
val seeker = persons.toSeeker
  .seek(_.lastName.asc)
  .seek(_.firstName.asc)
  .seek(_.id.asc)

docs.title: PostgreSQL Tuple Optimization
docs.text:
toSeeker seekers compare their columns as one row value, WHERE (name, id) > (?, ?), on PostgreSQL and H2 when every seek column is non-null and they all sort in the same direction. Nothing to choose; see Row Value Comparisons.

toPgTupleSeekerAsc / toPgTupleSeekerDesc are deprecated since 0.7.2 and will be removed before 1.0. On PostgreSQL toSeeker generates the same row value comparison, with cursor values bound as parameters instead of literals; replace them with toSeeker and give each column its direction:

// Before
val seeker = users.toPgTupleSeekerAsc.seek(_.name).seek(_.id)

// After
val seeker = users.toSeeker.seek(_.name.asc).seek(_.id.asc)

The tuple seeker sorts every column by its own value. If a SeekOrder is in scope for a column's type, toSeeker sorts that column by the SeekOrder instead, a different order with different cursors: keep the column's own order with .seek(_.status.asc)(seekerSortKeyIdentity), or bring the SeekOrder out of scope. Cursors of the tuple seeker can't be reused across the switch either way.

docs.title: Custom Cursor Environments
docs.text: Following are only examples and not meant to copy as-is. Adjust for your use case.

docs.title: Identity (Testing)
docs.text:
Useful for debugging - no encoding:

trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits {
    override implicit val cursorEnvironment: CursorEnvironment[JsValue] =
      CursorEnvironment(jsonCursorCodec, IdentityDecorator())
  }

  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}
// Cursor looks like: >[1,"Alice"]

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
import java.io._
import java.util.zip._

class GzipDecorator(inner: CursorDecorator = IdentityDecorator()) 
  extends CursorDecorator {

  override def encode(value: String): String = {
    val innerEncoded = inner.encode(value)
    val bytes = innerEncoded.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
    val out = new ByteArrayOutputStream()
    val gzip = new GZIPOutputStream(out)
    gzip.write(bytes)
    gzip.close()
    out.toByteArray.map("%02x".format(_)).mkString
  }

  override def decode(cursor: String): Either[Throwable, String] = {
    Try {
      val bytes = cursor.grouped(2).map(Integer.parseInt(_, 16).toByte).toArray
      val in = new GZIPInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes))
      val result = new String(in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
      in.close()
      result
    }.toEither.flatMap(inner.decode)
  }
}

trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits {
    override implicit val cursorEnvironment: CursorEnvironment[JsValue] =
      CursorEnvironment(jsonCursorCodec, Base64Decorator(GzipDecorator()))
  }

  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

docs.title: HMAC Signing (Prevent Tampering)
docs.text:
Recommended for production - prevents users from crafting malicious cursors:

import javax.crypto._
import javax.crypto.spec._

class HMACDecorator(
  secret: String,
  inner: CursorDecorator = IdentityDecorator()
) extends CursorDecorator {

  private def hmacSha256(data: String, key: String): String = {
    val mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256")
    mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), "HmacSHA256"))
    mac.doFinal(data.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
      .map("%02x".format(_))
      .mkString
  }

  override def encode(value: String): String = {
    val innerEncoded = inner.encode(value)
    val signature = hmacSha256(innerEncoded, secret)
    s"$signature:$innerEncoded"
  }

  override def decode(cursor: String): Either[Throwable, String] = {
    cursor.split(":", 2) match {
      case Array(sig, data) if sig == hmacSha256(data, secret) =>
        inner.decode(data)
      case _ =>
        Left(new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid cursor signature"))
    }
  }
}

trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits {
    override implicit val cursorEnvironment: CursorEnvironment[JsValue] =
      CursorEnvironment(jsonCursorCodec, Base64Decorator(HMACDecorator("your-secret-key")))
  }

  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
For sensitive data in cursors:

import javax.crypto._
import javax.crypto.spec._

class AESDecorator(
  key: String,
  inner: CursorDecorator = IdentityDecorator()
) extends CursorDecorator {

  private val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding")
  private val secretKey = new SecretKeySpec(
    key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).take(16), 
    "AES"
  )

  override def encode(value: String): String = {
    val innerEncoded = inner.encode(value)
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey)
    val encrypted = cipher.doFinal(innerEncoded.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))
    val iv = cipher.getIV
    (iv ++ encrypted).map("%02x".format(_)).mkString
  }

  override def decode(cursor: String): Either[Throwable, String] = {
    Try {
      val bytes = cursor.grouped(2).map(Integer.parseInt(_, 16).toByte).toArray
      val iv = bytes.take(16)
      val encrypted = bytes.drop(16)
      cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, secretKey, new IvParameterSpec(iv))
      val decrypted = cipher.doFinal(encrypted)
      new String(decrypted, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
    }.toEither.flatMap(inner.decode)
  }
}

trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits {
    override implicit val cursorEnvironment: CursorEnvironment[JsValue] =
      CursorEnvironment(jsonCursorCodec, Base64Decorator(AESDecorator("my-secret-key-16")))
  }

  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

docs.title: Invalid Cursors
docs.text:
def safePagenate(
  seeker: SlickSeeker[_, User, _, _, _],
  cursor: Option[String],
  limit: Int
): Future[Either[String, PaginatedResult[User]]] = {

  Future {
    db.run(seeker.page(limit, cursor))
  }.map(Right(_))
   .recover {
     case e: IllegalArgumentException => 
       Left(s"Invalid cursor: ${e.getMessage}")
     case e =>
       Left(s"Database error: ${e.getMessage}")
   }
}

docs.title: Cursor Expiration
docs.text:
case class ExpiringCursor(
  values: Seq[JsValue],
  expiresAt: Long
)

class ExpiringCursorCodec extends CursorCodec[JsValue] {
  def encode(values: Seq[JsValue]): String = {
    val cursor = ExpiringCursor(
      values,
      System.currentTimeMillis() + 3600000  // 1 hour
    )
    Json.stringify(Json.toJson(cursor))
  }

  def decode(cursor: String): Either[String, Seq[JsValue]] = {
    Try(Json.parse(cursor).as[ExpiringCursor]).toEither
      .left.map(e => s"Invalid cursor: ${e.getMessage}")
      .flatMap { c =>
        if (System.currentTimeMillis() > c.expiresAt) {
          Left("Cursor expired")
        } else {
          Right(c.values)
        }
      }
  }
}

trait MyProfile extends PostgresProfile with SlickSeekerSupport {
  implicit val cursorEnv: CursorEnvironment[JsValue] = 
    CursorEnvironment(ExpiringCursorCodec(), Base64Decorator())
}

docs.title: Test Pagination Completeness
docs.text:
class UserPaginationSpec extends AnyWordSpec {
  "paginate through all users" in {
    val seeker = users.toSeeker
      .seek(_.name.asc)
      .seek(_.id.asc)

    def getAllPages(
      cursor: Option[String] = None,
      acc: Seq[User] = Seq.empty
    ): Future[Seq[User]] = {
      db.run(seeker.page(10, cursor)).flatMap { page =>
        val allItems = acc ++ page.items
        page.nextCursor match {
          case Some(next) => getAllPages(Some(next), allItems)
          case None => Future.successful(allItems)
        }
      }
    }

    val allPaginated = await(getAllPages())
    val allDirect = await(db.run(users.result))

    allPaginated should contain theSameElementsInOrderAs allDirect
  }
}

docs.title: Test Bidirectional Consistency
docs.text:
"forward and backward pagination should be consistent" in {
  val seeker = users.toSeeker.seek(_.name.asc).seek(_.id.asc)

  // Go forward
  val p1 = await(db.run(seeker.page(5, None)))
  val p2 = await(db.run(seeker.page(5, p1.nextCursor)))
  val p3 = await(db.run(seeker.page(5, p2.nextCursor)))

  // Go backward
  val back2 = await(db.run(seeker.page(5, p3.prevCursor)))
  val back1 = await(db.run(seeker.page(5, back2.prevCursor)))

  // Should match
  back2.items shouldBe p2.items
  back1.items shouldBe p1.items
}

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get started with Slick Seeker in 5 minutes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your build.sbt:

libraryDependencies ++= Seq(
  "io.github.devnico" %% "slick-seeker" % "0.7.2",
  "io.github.devnico" %% "slick-seeker-play-json" % "0.7.2"  // Optional
)

docs.title: Step 1: Create Your Profile
docs.text:
Create a custom profile that extends your database profile and mixes in SlickSeekerSupport:

import slick.jdbc.PostgresProfile
import io.github.devnico.slickseeker.SlickSeekerSupport
import io.github.devnico.slickseeker.playjson.PlayJsonSeekerSupport

trait MyPostgresProfile extends PostgresProfile 
  with SlickSeekerSupport 
  with PlayJsonSeekerSupport {

  object MyApi extends JdbcAPI with SeekImplicits with JsonSeekerImplicits

  override val api: MyApi.type = MyApi
}

object MyPostgresProfile extends MyPostgresProfile

Why? This pattern allows Slick Seeker to work with any JDBC profile (PostgreSQL, MySQL, H2, SQLite, Oracle, etc.) without being tied to a specific database. By defining the cursor environment inside your profile, it's available wherever you import the profile API.

docs.title: Step 2: Import Your Profile API
docs.text:
// Import your custom profile API
import MyPostgresProfile.api._

This provides:

  • All Slick query methods (filter, sortBy, map, etc.)
  • Slick Seeker's .toSeeker extension method
  • All necessary type classes and implicits
  • Your cursor environment

docs.title: Step 3: Define Your Table
docs.text:
case class User(id: Int, name: String, email: String, active: Boolean)

class Users(tag: Tag) extends Table[User](tag, "users") {
  def id = column[Int]("id", O.PrimaryKey, O.AutoInc)
  def name = column[String]("name")
  def email = column[String]("email")
  def active = column[Boolean]("active")

  def * = (id, name, email, active).mapTo[User]
}

val users = TableQuery[Users]

docs.title: Step 4: Create a Seeker
docs.text:
val seeker = users.toSeeker
  .seek(_.name.asc)      // Primary sort: name ascending
  .seek(_.id.asc)        // Tiebreaker: id ascending

docs.title: Step 5: Paginate
docs.text:
import scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext.Implicits.global

// First page
val page1: Future[PaginatedResult[User]] = 
  db.run(seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = None))

// Next page (use cursor from previous page)
val page2: Future[PaginatedResult[User]] = 
  page1.flatMap { p1 =>
    db.run(seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = p1.nextCursor))
  }

// Previous page (bidirectional navigation)
val backToPage1: Future[PaginatedResult[User]] =
  page2.flatMap { p2 =>
    db.run(seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = p2.prevCursor))
  }

docs.title: PaginatedResult
docs.text:
The page() method returns a PaginatedResult[T]:

case class PaginatedResult[T](
  total: Int,              // Total number of items
  items: Seq[T],           // Current page items
  nextCursor: Option[String],  // Cursor for next page (None if last page)
  prevCursor: Option[String]   // Cursor for previous page (None if first page)
)

docs.title: PaginatedResultWithoutCount
docs.text:
The pageWithoutCount() method returns a PaginatedResultWithoutCount[T], skipping the COUNT(*) query. This is useful when the total count is not needed (e.g., infinite scroll UIs).

case class PaginatedResultWithoutCount[T](
  items: Seq[T],           // Current page items
  nextCursor: Option[String],  // Cursor for next page (None if last page)
  prevCursor: Option[String]   // Cursor for previous page (None if first page)
)

Usage:

// Without count (faster — no COUNT(*) query)
val page1: Future[PaginatedResultWithoutCount[User]] =
  db.run(seeker.pageWithoutCount(limit = 20, cursor = None))

// Convert between result types
val withCount: PaginatedResult[User] = page1WithoutCount.withCount(100)
val withoutCount: PaginatedResultWithoutCount[User] = fullResult.withoutCount

Cursors are fully interoperable — a cursor from page() works with pageWithoutCount() and vice versa.

docs.title: Using with Play JSON
docs.text:
For REST APIs, you can serialize PaginatedResult to JSON:

import io.github.devnico.slickseeker.playjson._
import play.api.libs.json.Json

implicit val userFormat = Json.format[User]

val result: PaginatedResult[User] = ???
val json = Json.toJson(result)

//   "items": [...],
//   "nextCursor": "eyJkaXJlY3Rpb24iOiJmb3J3YXJkIiwiLi4u",
//   "prevCursor": null

val seeker = users.toSeeker
  .seek(_.active.desc)    // Active users first
  .seek(_.name.asc)       // Then by name
  .seek(_.id.asc)         // Tiebreaker

docs.text:
case class Person(id: Int, firstName: String, lastName: Option[String])

val seeker = persons.toSeeker
  .seek(_.lastName.nullsLast.asc)  // NULLs at the end
  .seek(_.firstName.asc)
  .seek(_.id.asc)

docs.text:
// Sort descending
val seeker = users.toSeeker
  .seek(_.name.desc)
  .seek(_.id.desc)

// Or use seekDirection
val seeker2 = users.toSeeker
  .seek(_.name)
  .seek(_.id)
  .seekDirection(SortDirection.Desc)

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: On PostgreSQL (and H2), toSeeker compares non-null seek columns that all sort the same way as one row value, WHERE (name, id) > (?, ?), which uses a composite index directly. See Row Value Comparisons.

docs.title: API Quick Reference
docs.text:
// Standard seeker
users.toSeeker
  .seek(_.col.asc)           // Ascending
  .seek(_.col.desc)          // Descending
  .seek(_.col.nullsLast.asc) // Nulls handling
  .seekDirection(...)        // Batch direction change

// Pagination
seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = None)                    // With total count
seeker.page(limit = 20, cursor = Some("..."))              // Next/prev page
seeker.pageWithoutCount(limit = 20, cursor = None)         // Without total count
